lessons.title: Elastic models, equilibrium and changes of load
lessons.summary: Distinguish natural length, extension, modulus and the actual resultant force.
lessons.objective: Build a correct Hookean force model and interpret an equilibrium or a change of load.
lessons.before: Review resolving forces and the contact-force lesson. Numerical examples use g=10 m s⁻² where stated. For the energy parts of the written load-change questions, continue with elastic energy before attempting those parts.
lessons.ideas:
Length and extension are different measurements

Let ℓ₀ be natural length, ℓ the current end separation and x=ℓ−ℓ₀ the signed extension. For a light Hookean spring kept straight, the restoring force has magnitude λ|x|/ℓ₀, where λ is its modulus. It pulls when extended and pushes when compressed. The signed force opposes the displacement from natural length.

\[\begin{gathered}k_s=\frac{\lambda}{\ell_0}\\F_{\rm restoring}=-k_s x\end{gathered}\]

Modulus λ has units N, while stiffness kₛ has units N m⁻¹. They are not interchangeable. Cutting a uniform string into two equal material parts retains the same modulus but halves each natural length, so each part has twice the original stiffness.

An elastic string cannot push

\[\begin{gathered}T=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\lambda(\ell-\ell_0)}{\ell_0},&\ell\ge\ell_0,\\0,&\ell\lt\ell_0.\end{cases}\end{gathered}\]

A string shorter than its natural length is slack. Do not extend the tension formula to a negative force. A guided spring can instead remain straight during compression. State which object and guide the question specifies; they can lead to different turning points.

Equilibrium is a force condition

A hanging particle in vertical equilibrium has T=mg, giving extension mgℓ₀/λ. On a smooth slope, resolve the weight along the slope. Under a horizontal holding force as well as weight, the tension is the resultant magnitude and its direction follows from the force components. Do not put T=mg for every sloping string.

Changing the load does not instantly change the length

If a load is attached while the particle is held and then released, calculate the new equilibrium using the new moving mass. The release position is the old length, not the new equilibrium length. Removing a load without an impulse leaves the remaining particle's instantaneous velocity unchanged, but its acceleration generally changes.

A useful energy preview

For a straight smooth hanging spring, measuring signed displacement q downwards from its new equilibrium completes the square in the total potential. If released from rest at q=D,

\[\begin{gathered}\frac12mv^2+\frac12k_s q^2=\frac12k_s D^2\end{gathered}\]

This is an energy identity, derived in the next lesson. It is valid only while that same spring model remains valid. For a string, check that the entire proposed path stays stretched; otherwise use a separate slack stage.

Circular motion is a separate force application

For an elastic conical pendulum, first use vertical and radial components, then Hooke's law to find length. The actual orbit radius is ℓ sinθ. The conical-pendulum lesson gives the derivation. Non-degenerate motion excludes zero radius, which can make the lower endpoint of an angular-speed interval strict.
lessons.method:
1. Choose spring or tension-only string, and identify its actual natural length.
  2. Draw forces and use the correct signed extension in Hooke’s law.
  3. For equilibrium, resolve forces before finding length or modulus.
  4. After a load change, distinguish the old release position from the new equilibrium.
  5. Check extension, guide/contact conditions, units and any strict geometric bounds.
mistakes: Use extension, not total length, in the force law.
Modulus is a force; stiffness is force per unit length.
A shortened string is slack, not compressed.
Removing mass changes the force balance even without an impulse.
A nonzero circular orbit excludes the vertically hanging limiting state.

examples.title: 1 · Calibrate an unknown natural length
examples.question: A hanging spring has length 1.3 m under a 10 N load and 1.9 m under a 30 N load. The same Hookean law holds in both trials. Find its stiffness, natural length and modulus.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}k_s=\frac{30-10}{1.9-1.3}=\frac{100}3\\\ell_0=\frac{13}{10}-\frac{10}{100/3}=1\\\lambda=k_s\ell_0=\frac{100}3\end{gathered}\]

The stiffness is \(\frac{100}3\) N m⁻¹ and the modulus is \(\frac{100}3\) N. Their equal numerical values here result from the 1 m natural length, not from equal units.

examples.title: 2 · A horizontal force changes the tension
examples.question: A particle of weight 15 N is held by an 8 N horizontal force on a string of natural length \(\frac65\) m and modulus 68 N, attached to a ceiling point. Find the tension and vertical depth below the ceiling.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}T=\sqrt{15^2+8^2}=17\\e=\frac{17}{68}\cdot\frac65=\frac3{10}\\\ell=\frac32\\\cos\theta=\frac{15}{17}\\h=\frac32\frac{15}{17}=\frac{45}{34}\end{gathered}\]

Both force components belong to the same tension. The vertical depth is the stretched length times the vertical direction cosine.

examples.title: 3 · A guided spring can supply thrust
examples.question: A spring stands vertically on a fixed base and is kept straight by a smooth guide. Its natural length is \(2a\) and modulus \(8mg\). A mass m rests on its upper end. Find its equilibrium compression and length.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac{8mg}{2a}c=mg\\c=\frac a4\\\ell=2a-c=\frac74a\end{gathered}\]

The spring pushes upwards when compressed. A tension-only string could not support this configuration in the same way.

examples.title: 4 · Attach a load without an impact
examples.question: A mass m hangs at rest from a string of natural length a and modulus \(6mg\). While held at that length, another mass m is attached. The combined mass is released from rest. Find its greatest speed and greatest extension.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}e_0=\frac a6,\qquad e_{\rm eq}=\frac a3\\\frac12(2m)v_{\max}^2=\frac12\frac{6mg}{a}\left(\frac a6\right)^2\\v_{\max}=\sqrt{\frac{ag}{12}}\\e_{\max}=2e_{\rm eq}-e_0=\frac a2\end{gathered}\]

All proposed extensions are positive, so the string stays taut. There was no collision: energy is applied only after release, with the combined mass 2m.

lessons.title: Elastic energy, extension and compression
lessons.summary: Derive stored energy and combine it with gravity and kinetic energy over a valid stage.
lessons.objective: Use the work–energy principle to find speeds, extrema and physically admissible turning points.
lessons.before: Complete elastic force models. Review kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy and solving quadratics. A fixed smooth guide constrains direction but does no work along the allowed path.
lessons.ideas:
Stored energy is the work of a variable force

Increasing a spring extension slowly from zero to x requires work equal to the area under the force–extension graph. The graph is a straight line through the origin, so the area is a triangle. Equivalently, integrate the force:

\[\begin{gathered}U_e(x)=\int_0^x\frac{\lambda s}{\ell_0}\,ds\\U_e=\frac{\lambda x^2}{2\ell_0}=\frac12k_sx^2\end{gathered}\]

For a guided spring this is also positive during compression: signed x is negative but x² is positive. The spring's work between two states is the decrease of this energy. Force times final extension would give twice the stored energy, not the correct work.

A slack string stores no elastic energy

\[\begin{gathered}U_e(\ell)=\frac{\lambda}{2\ell_0}\big(\max(\ell-\ell_0,0)\big)^2\end{gathered}\]

Use current separation to decide whether the string is taut. Crossing natural length does not necessarily stop the particle. Its tension and elastic energy then become zero, while speed remains continuous in an ideal non-impulsive transition.

Write one consistent energy balance

\[\begin{gathered}K_i+V_i+W_{\rm applied}=K_f+V_f+W_{\rm lost}\\K=\frac12mv^2,\qquad V=mg y+\sum U_e\end{gathered}\]

Use upward height y for gravitational potential. Work lost to sliding friction is positive in the loss term. When travelling up a slope, the height rise is distance times the sine of inclination. Energy depends on speed squared; it does not tell you the direction of velocity without the stated motion.

Turning points require a reachable root

At a turning point v=0. One root often reproduces the starting point, so select the next point in the direction of travel. Check the force model and geometry on the intervening path. For a vertical spring, use signed extension x downwards from natural length:

\[\begin{gathered}V(x)=\frac12k_sx^2-mgx\\x_{\rm eq}=\frac{mg}{k_s}\\V(x)=\frac12k_s(x-x_{\rm eq})^2-\frac{(mg)^2}{2k_s}\end{gathered}\]

Equal-potential turning points of this same spring stage lie equally far from equilibrium. This energy observation needs no time-dependent oscillation formula. It cannot be used through a slack-string interval as if the string were a compressible spring.

Maximum speed is minimum reachable potential

On a smooth stage, speed is greatest where potential is smallest along the actual allowed path. Check force balance at an interior candidate and compare any boundaries. In a multi-stage problem, compare candidates from every stage. Use force balance again for acceleration; a large speed does not imply a large acceleration.
lessons.method:
1. State the coordinate, natural length and active elastic branches.
  2. Write kinetic, gravitational and every elastic energy with one reference.
  3. Include applied work and friction losses with consistent signs.
  4. Solve for every requested speed or turning point, rejecting unreachable roots.
  5. Check maximum-speed candidates and obtain acceleration from the actual resultant.
mistakes: Stored energy is half force times extension for a Hookean element.
Compression has positive stored energy, not negative energy.
A string has zero energy and force while slack.
The old release point is not the next turning point.
Maximum speed and maximum spring force generally occur at different positions.

examples.title: 1 · Work is an energy difference
examples.question: A spring has natural length \(\frac45\) m and modulus 40 N. Find its force magnitude and stored energy at extension \(\frac3{10}\) m, and the work needed to increase extension from \(\frac1{10}\) m to \(\frac3{10}\) m.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}k_s=\frac{40}{4/5}=50\\T=50\left(\frac3{10}\right)=15\\U_e=\frac12(50)\left(\frac3{10}\right)^2=\frac94\\W=U_e(3/10)-U_e(1/10)\\W=\frac12(50)\left(\frac9{100}-\frac1{100}\right)=2\end{gathered}\]

The force is 15 N, the stored energy is 9/4 J and the work over the stated interval is 2 J. The final force is not constant during the extension.

examples.title: 2 · The next stop can involve compression
examples.question: A guided vertical spring of natural length a and modulus \(6mg\) hangs from a fixed point and carries a mass m. It is released from rest at length \(\frac32a\). Find the next turning length and greatest speed.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x_{\rm eq}=\frac a6,\qquad x_0=\frac a2\\x_1=2x_{\rm eq}-x_0=-\frac a6\\\ell_{\min}=a+x_1=\frac56a\\v_{\max}^2=\frac{6g}{a}\left(\frac a3\right)^2=\frac23ag\end{gathered}\]

The spring is compressed at the next stop. This is permitted by its guide. Replacing it by a string would change the motion after natural length was crossed.

examples.title: 3 · Choose the physical quadratic root
examples.question: A string has natural length a and modulus \(5mg\). A particle of mass m is projected down a smooth slope from natural length with speed \(\sqrt{\frac25ag}\). The inclination has sine \(\frac35\). Find its greatest extension.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac15mga+\frac35mgx=\frac{5mg}{2a}x^2\\z=\frac xa,\qquad25z^2-6z-2=0\\z=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{59}}{25}\\x=\frac{3+\sqrt{59}}{25}a\end{gathered}\]

The negative algebraic root is outside this stretched-string stage. Potential decreases first and then increases, so the positive root is the first stop on the descent.

examples.title: 4 · Recover a modulus from two moving states
examples.question: On a smooth horizontal guide, a mass m moves away from a fixed end. Its string has natural length a. Speed is \(\sqrt{3ag}\) at length \(\frac54a\), and \(\sqrt{2ag}\) at length \(\frac32a\). Find the modulus and the tension at the second point.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\Delta K=\frac12m(3ag-2ag)=\frac12mga\\\Delta U_e=\frac{\lambda}{2a}\left(\frac{a^2}4-\frac{a^2}{16}\right)\\\Delta K=\Delta U_e\\\lambda=\frac{16}3mg\\T=\lambda\frac{a/2}{a}=\frac83mg\end{gathered}\]

Both states are stretched and are in the same smooth stage. The increase in elastic energy equals the decrease in kinetic energy.

lessons.title: Coupled elements, geometry and friction
lessons.summary: Sum all elastic energies, then test the geometry and the friction required at rest.
lessons.objective: Solve linked elastic systems with correct half-string properties, separate forces and work losses.
lessons.before: Complete Hookean force models and work and stored energy. Review sliding and static friction. Read every member’s natural length and modulus separately.
lessons.ideas:
Each element has its own extension

For a particle between anchors A and B separated by D, let q=AP. The member lengths are q and D−q. Tensions can be equal on a horizontal table in equilibrium, but a vertical system needs their difference to balance weight. A spring may push; a slack string contributes zero.

\[\begin{gathered}U_e=\sum_i\frac{\lambda_i x_i^2}{2\ell_{0i}}\end{gathered}\]

The displayed sum is for active springs or stretched strings. Use the positive-extension branch for strings. Write the force law before solving and check that every assumed taut member has positive extension.

A midpoint attachment halves natural length, not modulus

For a uniform string fixed at its midpoint to a particle, each material half keeps the original modulus but has half the original natural length. In a symmetric geometry the half-length is found by Pythagoras. Add the energies of both halves; do not count only one. Equal tensions can cancel at a collinear position despite nonzero stored energy.

Symmetric does not mean that tension equals weight

For a particle a distance y below the mid-level of equal supports at horizontal half-separation b, each half-string has length L=√(b²+y²). Vertical equilibrium requires

\[\begin{gathered}2T\frac yL=mg\end{gathered}\]

After release, replace vertical balance by Newton’s second law or use the energy of both halves with gravity. An ideal rigid rod or smooth guide can constrain the path without doing work, but can still have a nonzero reaction. A holding force removed before motion must not be included in the later energy balance.

Sliding friction dissipates energy

\[\begin{gathered}W_{\rm lost}=\int\mu N\,ds\end{gathered}\]

On a horizontal table with only weight and vertical normal, N=mg and the loss is μmg times distance travelled. On a slope with no other normal components, N=mg cosα. If a string or applied force changes the normal, calculate N first. Friction reverses when motion reverses.

A first stop is not necessarily permanent rest

At a stopping point, recompute the friction needed for static equilibrium. It may be smaller than its maximum and may point in a different direction from the preceding sliding friction. Permanent rest is possible only if the required magnitude is at most μN. A nonzero spring force does not by itself imply that motion restarts.

Check the whole path

A both-taut quadratic energy model may cease to apply before the next stop. Identify natural-length boundaries and switch the relevant term off. Conversely, a guided spring remains energetic through compression. Geometric symmetry is a constraint to verify, not permission to ignore one of the forces.
lessons.method:
1. Express all lengths from one coordinate and calculate each actual extension.
  2. Resolve forces for equilibrium or an instantaneous acceleration.
  3. Add every active elastic energy and the gravitational term.
  4. Subtract work lost along the travelled path, splitting branches when needed.
  5. At each stop check static friction, tautness, geometry and the next possible event.
mistakes: Equal modulus does not mean equal stiffness for different natural lengths.
Each half of a uniform string has the same modulus as the whole material.
Include both half-string energies in a symmetric system.
Sliding friction and the friction required for final rest need not be equal.
A both-taut formula is valid only while both extensions remain non-negative.

examples.title: 1 · Two springs share one displacement
examples.question: A mass m lies between anchors \(5a\) apart on a smooth horizontal guide. The left spring has natural length a and modulus \(2mg\); the right has natural length \(2a\) and modulus \(4mg\). Find equilibrium and the greatest speed after a displacement \(\frac a4\) from it and release from rest.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}z=\frac qa\\2(z-1)=2(3-z)\\q_{\rm eq}=2a,\qquad T=2mg\\k_{\rm total}=\frac{4mg}{a}\\\frac12mv_{\max}^2=\frac12\frac{4mg}{a}\left(\frac a4\right)^2\\v_{\max}=\frac12\sqrt{ag}\end{gathered}\]

Both springs have positive extension throughout this small motion. The greatest speed occurs at the minimum of their combined potential, not where either spring alone has natural length.

examples.title: 2 · A vertical system needs a difference of tensions
examples.question: Anchors A above B are \(10a\) apart. A particle of mass km lies between them. The upper string has natural length \(2a\) and modulus \(4mg\); the lower has natural length \(3a\) and modulus \(3mg\). Find BP in equilibrium and the full k-range for both strings to be stretched. For k=1, give both tensions.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}z=\frac{BP}{a}\\\frac{T_U}{mg}=2(8-z),\qquad\frac{T_L}{mg}=z-3\\2(8-z)-(z-3)=k\\BP=\frac{19-k}{3}a\\3\lt z\lt8\quad\Longrightarrow\quad0\lt k\lt10\\k=1:\qquad T_U=4mg,\quad T_L=3mg\end{gathered}\]

The lower string pulls downwards, along with weight. Both-taut endpoints are excluded because an extension becomes zero there; k is positive by definition.

examples.title: 3 · Sliding stops before the string becomes slack
examples.question: A mass m on a rough horizontal table is joined to a string of natural length a and modulus \(4mg\). It is released at extension \(\frac a2\). Sliding and limiting static coefficients are both \(\frac32\). Find its extension at the first stop and decide whether it stays there.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}T_0=2mg\gt\frac32mg\\z=\frac xa\\2\left(\frac14-z^2\right)=\frac32\left(\frac12-z\right)\\x=\frac a2\quad\text{or}\quad x=\frac a4\\T_{\rm stop}=mg\lt\frac32mg\end{gathered}\]

The second root is the next stop; the release root must be discarded. The final friction required is mg outwards, below its allowed maximum, so the particle remains at rest with the string stretched. A coefficient greater than one is physically permitted in this ideal model.

examples.title: 4 · Two half-strings and a vertical launch
examples.question: Equal supports are \(6a\) apart. A uniform elastic string of natural length \(4a\) is fixed between them with a mass m attached to its material midpoint. It hangs \(4a\) below the support level in equilibrium. Find its modulus and stored elastic energy. If launched vertically upwards from equilibrium at speed \(\sqrt{6ag}\), find its speed when it first reaches support level.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}L_{\rm eq}=5a,\qquad \ell_{0,\rm half}=2a\\2T\frac45=mg,\qquad T=\frac58mg\\\lambda=T\frac{2a}{3a}=\frac5{12}mg\\U_{\rm eq}=2\frac{\lambda(3a)^2}{4a}=\frac{15}8mga\\U_M=2\frac{\lambda a^2}{4a}=\frac5{24}mga\\\frac{v_M^2}{2ag}=3+\frac{15}8-4-\frac5{24}\\v_M^2=\frac43ag\end{gathered}\]

Each half retains modulus λ. Potential increases towards support level during this ascent, so positive speed there rules out an earlier stop. The equal tensions are horizontal and opposite at that instant.

lessons.title: Slack phases, collisions and changes of force
lessons.summary: Use a new model at natural length, an impact or the boundary of a rough region.
lessons.objective: Track position and speed between valid elastic stages and select the first reachable event.
lessons.before: Complete elastic energy and coupled systems and friction. Direct collisions use signed momentum and restitution, as explained in the circular-motion stages lesson. This lesson uses energy and force balance, without time-dependent oscillation formulas.
lessons.ideas:
Natural length is a model boundary for a string

At ℓ=ℓ₀ the tension and elastic energy are zero. If motion continues to shorter separation, use only the forces still active. Under vertical gravity a free particle can continue upwards, slowing until its speed is zero. Position and speed are continuous at an ideal slackening transition; do not remove its remaining kinetic energy.

Passing the fixed end changes geometry

If the question expressly allows passage through an ideal attachment point, let q be a signed coordinate along its guide. String separation is |q|, not q. The string is slack for |q|<ℓ₀, then can stretch on the other side. Its pull is always towards the fixed end.

\[\begin{gathered}U_e(q)=\frac{\lambda}{2\ell_0}\big(\max(|q|-\ell_0,0)\big)^2\end{gathered}\]

Include the gravitational term with the sign of the chosen coordinate. Evaluate maximum-speed candidates on each active branch and at the boundaries. Never turn a negative coordinate automatically into a negative extension.

An impact is not a smooth energy stage

For two particles that stick together, conserve momentum along the impact line if there is no external impulse in that direction:

\[\begin{gathered}m_1u_1+m_2u_2=(m_1+m_2)V\end{gathered}\]

Use the total moving mass afterwards, and subtract the collision energy loss before the subsequent smooth spring motion. A finite spring force does not supply an instantaneous impulse during an ideal direct collision. Adding a stationary load while holding a position is a different process: no impact velocity calculation is required.

A force discontinuity need not cause a velocity jump

At the edge of a rough strip with no step or impact, speed remains continuous. Friction switches on and the acceleration changes immediately. Calculate the smooth-side and rough-side resultants separately. Continue energy with friction work only over the rough distance travelled.

Use a timeline and test all event candidates

Label the release, each natural-length crossing, each collision, the support point and the next stop. State which event happens first and which energy terms survive. If an energy equation gives two positions with the same speed, choose the one encountered first in the stated direction. Check that no earlier zero speed or invalid contact interrupts the path.
lessons.method:
1. Locate the first boundary of the current physical model.
  2. Carry position and speed continuously through a non-impulsive transition.
  3. At a collision use impulse laws, then restart energy with the new moving mass.
  4. Activate only the forces and energies valid on the new stage.
  5. Check first-event order, both coordinate signs, static friction and all requested extrema.
mistakes: A slack string has neither compressive force nor compressive energy.
Use absolute separation for a string when the particle passes its fixed end.
Do not conserve kinetic energy across a coalescing collision.
At a rough boundary speed can be continuous while acceleration jumps.
Select the first equal-speed passage, not merely any algebraic root.

examples.title: 1 · Rise continues after tension disappears
examples.question: A string of natural length a and modulus \(4mg\) supports masses m and 2m together in equilibrium. The 2m load is removed without an impulse. For the remaining particle, find the speed at natural length, least length in its first ascent and initial acceleration.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}e_0=\frac{3a}4,\qquad U_0=\frac98mga\\\frac12mv_N^2=\frac98mga-\frac34mga=\frac38mga\\v_N^2=\frac34ag\\\Delta h_{\rm slack}=\frac{v_N^2}{2g}=\frac38a\\\ell_{\min}=\frac58a\\a_0=\frac{3mg-mg}{m}=2g\quad\text{upwards}\end{gathered}\]

The upper stop occurs below the fixed end, so the separation stays positive. The string is slack between natural length and that stop; its remaining kinetic energy is converted into gravitational potential.

examples.title: 2 · A string stretches on the other side of its anchor
examples.question: A particle moves on a smooth straight incline with sine \(\frac12\). A string of natural length a and modulus \(4mg\) joins it to O, which it may pass unobstructed. It starts at rest \(\frac32a\) uphill of O. Find the position and value of greatest speed on its first descent.
examples.solution:
Let q be signed distance downhill from O.

\[\begin{gathered}z=\frac qa\\p(z)=\max(|z|-1,0)\\\frac{V(z)}{mga}=2p(z)^2-\frac z2\\\frac{V_0}{mga}=\frac12+\frac34=\frac54\\4(z-1)-\frac12=0,\qquad z=\frac98\\\frac{V_{\min}}{mga}=-\frac{17}{32}\\v_{\max}^2=\frac{57}{16}ag\end{gathered}\]

Potential decreases through the uphill taut segment and the whole slack segment, then reaches its minimum 9a/8 downhill of O. The greatest speed is \(\frac{\sqrt{57}}4\sqrt{ag}\). Using a negative signed extension while passing O would give an incorrect spring model.

examples.title: 3 · Momentum first, compression afterwards
examples.question: A particle of mass m strikes a stationary mass 2m attached to a horizontal guided spring at natural length. The incoming velocity towards the fixed end is \(3\sqrt{ag}\). They stick together. The spring has natural length a and modulus \(9mg\). Find the shared speed, greatest compression and kinetic energy lost in impact.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}m(3\sqrt{ag})=3mV\\V=\sqrt{ag}\\\frac12(3m)V^2=\frac{9mg}{2a}c^2\\c=\frac a{\sqrt3}\\K_{\rm lost}=\frac12m(3\sqrt{ag})^2-\frac12(3m)V^2\\K_{\rm lost}=3mga\end{gathered}\]

The spring was initially unstressed, and the collision has no external impulse along the guide. Only the post-impact kinetic energy can be converted into elastic energy.

examples.title: 4 · Entering a rough strip changes acceleration
examples.question: A mass m starts at natural length of a guided spring of length a and modulus \(4mg\), moving towards its fixed end at speed \(\sqrt{2ag}\). The table is smooth until compression reaches \(\frac a4\), then has sliding coefficient \(\frac12\). There is no step or impact. Find the speed squared and deceleration on each side of entry, then the greatest compression.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v_C^2=2ag-4g\frac{(a/4)^2}{a}=\frac74ag\\d_-=g,\qquad d_+=\frac32g\\z=\frac ca,\qquad1=2z^2+\frac12\left(z-\frac14\right)\\16z^2+4z-9=0\\c=\frac{\sqrt{37}-1}{8}a\end{gathered}\]

Speed is continuous at C, but the friction adds g/2 to the deceleration. The selected root lies beyond a/4 and before compression a; the negative root is not on this path. The energy loss counts only the rough distance after C.

questions.title: All calibration quantities
questions.prompt_html: A hanging spring has length \(\frac{13}{10}\) m under a \(10\) N load and length \(\frac{19}{10}\) m under a \(30\) N load. Find its stiffness in N m⁻¹, natural length in m and modulus in N.
questions.answer_html: Stiffness in N per m: \(\frac{100}{3}\); Natural length in m: \(1\); Modulus in N: \(\frac{100}{3}\)
questions.solution_html: The change in force divided by change in length is stiffness. Subtract the extension F/k from either measured length; modulus is stiffness times natural length.
questions.hint_html: Identify the natural length and whether the member can compress. Resolve the actual forces before applying Hooke’s law. Distinguish the release position from the new equilibrium after a load change.

questions.title: Tension, extension and vertical depth
questions.prompt_html: A particle of weight \(24\) N is held by a horizontal force \(7\) N and a string from a ceiling point. Natural length is \(\frac{4}{5}\) m and modulus \(100\) N. Give the tension, extension and vertical depth below the ceiling, in N, m and m.

The springs and particle lie along \(AB\). Let \(E\) be the equilibrium position. Both springs obey Hooke's law in extension and compression.

  1. Find \(AE\), and express the common spring tension at \(E\) in terms of \(\lambda\).

    [3]

  2. The particle is displaced \(0.2\,\mathrm m\) from \(E\) towards \(B\) and released from rest. Its speed at \(E\) is \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find \(\lambda\), using energy.

    [4]

  3. For the same motion, find the speed and the resultant force when the particle is \(0.12\,\mathrm m\) from \(E\) towards \(A\).

    [3]

  4. In a separate trial the particle is projected from \(E\). Find the greatest launch speed for which neither spring is compressed.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(AE=1.7\,\mathrm m\); common tension \(=5\lambda/12\,\mathrm N\).

(b)

\(\lambda=90\).

(c)

Speed \(1.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); force \(18\,\mathrm N\) towards \(E\).

(d)

\(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The stiffnesses are equal: \[k_A=\frac{\lambda}{1.2}=\frac{5\lambda}{6},\qquad k_B=\frac{(2/3)\lambda}{0.8}=\frac{5\lambda}{6}.\] Writing \(AE=s\), the extensions are \(s-1.2\) and \(2.2-s\). Equal tensions therefore give \(s-1.2=2.2-s\), so \(s=1.7\). Each extension is \(0.5\,\mathrm m\); hence each tension is \((5\lambda/6)(0.5)=5\lambda/12\,\mathrm N\).

Part (b)

For a displacement \(x\) towards \(B\), the extensions are \(0.5+x\) and \(0.5-x\). The increase in their total elastic energy above its value at \(E\) is \[\Delta U=\frac12\frac{5\lambda}{6}\big((0.5+x)^2+(0.5-x)^2-2(0.5)^2\big)=\frac{5\lambda}{6}x^2.\] At release this is \(\lambda/30\,\mathrm J\). It becomes kinetic energy at \(E\), so \[\frac{\lambda}{30}=\frac12(1.5)(2^2)=3.\] Thus \(\lambda=90\). Energy already stored at equilibrium is not all available for motion; only the energy difference is used.

Part (c)

Now each stiffness is \(75\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\), and energy gives \[\frac12(1.5)v^2+75x^2=3.\] At \(x=-0.12\), \(v^2=4-100(0.12)^2=2.56\), so \(v=1.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The signed resultant is \(75(0.5-x)-75(0.5+x)=-150x\). At \(x=-0.12\) this is \(+18\,\mathrm N\), towards \(B\), hence towards \(E\).

Part (d)

Neither spring is compressed precisely when \(|x|\leq0.5\). At a limiting turning point, \[\frac12(1.5)u^2=75(0.5)^2.\] Thus \(u^2=25\) and the greatest speed is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Equality is allowed: a spring may just reach natural length without compression.

questions.title: Two strings with alternating slack phases
questions.prompt_html:
Fixed points \(A\) and \(B\) are \(5a\) apart on a smooth horizontal table, where \(a\gt0\). A particle \(P\) of mass \(m\) is constrained by a smooth straight guide to move along \(AB\). It is joined to \(A\) by a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(mg\), and to \(B\) by another of natural length \(2a\) and modulus \(2mg\). Each string is slack when shorter than its natural length. The particle is held at \(AP=a/2\) and released from rest.

  1. Find the equilibrium position between \(A\) and \(B\), and the two tensions there.

    [3]

  2. Find the speed when \(AP=a\) for the first time.

    [3]

  3. While both strings are taut, put \(z=AP/a\). Obtain an expression for \(v^2\), and find the greatest speed during the motion.

    [4]

  4. Find \(AP\) when \(P\) next comes to rest. Explain why the both-taut formula must not be used up to this point.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(AP=2a\); both tensions are \(mg\).

(b)

\(\frac32\sqrt{ag}\).

(c)

\(v^2=ag\big(\frac{17}{4}-2(z-2)^2\big)\); greatest speed \(\frac{\sqrt{17}}2\sqrt{ag}\).

(d)

\(AP=7a/2\); the right string is slack after \(AP=3a\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Both strings have stiffness \(mg/a\). When both are stretched and \(AP=s\), their extensions are \(s-a\) and \(3a-s\). Force balance requires \(s-a=3a-s\), giving \(s=2a\). Both extensions are \(a\), so each tension is \(mg\). This position lies in the both-taut interval \(a\lt s\lt3a\).

Part (b)

Initially the left string is slack. The right string has extension \(5a-a/2-2a=5a/2\). Thus the initial energy is \[U_0=\frac{mg}{2a}\left(\frac{5a}{2}\right)^2=\frac{25}{8}mga.\] At \(AP=a\), the right extension is \(2a\) and the left elastic energy is still zero. Hence \[\frac12mv^2=\frac{25}{8}mga-2mga=\frac98mga,\] so \(v=\frac32\sqrt{ag}\).

Part (c)

For \(1\leq z\leq3\), \[U=\frac12mga\big((z-1)^2+(3-z)^2\big)=mga\big((z-2)^2+1\big).\] Subtracting from \(U_0=25mga/8\) gives the stated speed formula. The energy is least at \(z=2\), so the speed there is \(\sqrt{17ag}/2\).

Before \(z=1\), only the right string pulls the particle towards \(B\), and its speed increases. After \(z=3\), only the left string acts and its speed decreases. Therefore this is the greatest speed over the whole excursion, not just over the both-taut interval.

Part (d)

At \(z=3\), the speed is still \(3\sqrt{ag}/2\), so the particle continues beyond that point. The right string then becomes slack; it cannot store compression energy. The left string alone stores energy at the turning point: \[\frac{mg}{2a}(s-a)^2=\frac{25}{8}mga.\] Since \(s\gt3a\), take \(s-a=5a/2\), giving \(s=7a/2\). The kinetic energy is positive up to this point and the left tension opposes the motion, so this is the next stop. It lies before \(B\).

questions.title: Two vertical strings and an unknown mass
questions.prompt_html:
Fixed points \(A\) and \(B\) are \(15a\) apart, with \(A\) vertically above \(B\). A particle \(P\) of mass \(km\), where \(k\gt0\), lies on the vertical line between them. It is joined to \(A\) by a light elastic string of natural length \(3a\) and modulus \(6mg\), and to \(B\) by another of natural length \(5a\) and modulus \(5mg\).

  1. Find \(BP\) in equilibrium when both strings are stretched, and state the range of \(k\) for which this is possible.

    [3]

  2. The particle is held at \(BP=12a\) and released from rest. It next stops at \(BP=5a\). Find \(k\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(BP=(29-k)a/3\), with \(0\lt k\lt14\).

(b)

\(k=7/2\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(BP=za\). The upper extension is \((12-z)a\), giving tension \(2mg(12-z)\); the lower extension is \((z-5)a\), giving tension \(mg(z-5)\). Force balance gives \[2(12-z)-(z-5)-k=0,\] so \(z=(29-k)/3\). Both strings are stretched when \(5\lt z\lt12\). Combining this with \(k\gt0\) gives \(0\lt k\lt14\).

Part (b)

Initially the upper string is at natural length and the lower extension is \(7a\), so the elastic energy is \(49mga/2\). At the final point the lower string is at natural length and the upper extension is \(7a\), so the elastic energy is \(49mga\). The gravitational potential energy decreases by \(7kmga\). Thus \[\frac{49}{2}+7k=49,\] which gives \(k=7/2\).

For this value, the kinetic energy at an intermediate height is \[K=\frac32mga(12-z)(z-5).\] It is positive for \(5\lt z\lt12\), so no earlier stop occurs. Both strings are stretched throughout that open interval.
questions.hint_html: The upper string pulls upwards, while the lower string and the weight act downwards. The two endpoints are natural-length boundaries.

questions.title: A midpoint attachment moving across a table
questions.prompt_html:
A uniform light elastic string of natural length \(6a\) and modulus \(6mg\) has its ends fixed at points \(A\) and \(B\), \(8a\) apart on a smooth horizontal table. A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to its midpoint. Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(AB\). Initially the particle is held off the line \(AB\), with \(AP=BP=L\), then released. It moves along the perpendicular bisector and passes through \(M\) with speed \(\sqrt{12ag}\).

  1. Find \(L\).

    [4]

  2. Find the initial acceleration.

    [2]

  3. Find the tension in each half-string at \(M\), and explain why the resultant horizontal force is zero there despite the non-zero tensions.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(L=5a\).

(b)

\(24g/5\), towards \(M\).

(c)

Each tension is \(2mg\); the forces are equal and opposite along \(AB\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Each half-string has natural length \(3a\), modulus \(6mg\), and stiffness \(2mg/a\). The total elastic energy at a half-length \(l\) is therefore \[2\frac{6mg}{2(3a)}(l-3a)^2=\frac{2mg}{a}(l-3a)^2.\] At \(M\), each length is \(4a\), so elastic energy remains \(2mga\); it is not zero. Conservation of energy gives \[\frac{2mg}{a}(L-3a)^2-2mga=\frac12m(12ag)=6mga.\] Thus \((L-3a)^2=4a^2\). Geometry requires \(L\geq4a\), so \(L=5a\), not \(a\).

Part (b)

Initially \(MP=\sqrt{(5a)^2-(4a)^2}=3a\). Each tension is \((2mg/a)(2a)=4mg\). Its component towards \(M\) is \(4mg(3/5)\). The two such components add, so the acceleration is \(2(4mg)(3/5)/m=24g/5\), towards \(M\).

Part (c)

At \(M\), each extension is \(a\), so each tension is \(2mg\). The two string segments lie on the same straight line, on opposite sides of the particle. Their force vectors cancel even though each half is stretched and stores elastic energy. Zero resultant does not mean zero tension.
questions.hint_html: The string is still stretched at the midpoint between the fixed ends. Each half keeps the original modulus.

questions.title: An elastic conical pendulum and a force limit
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(4mg\). It moves steadily in a non-degenerate horizontal circle, with the string at \(60^\circ\) to the downward vertical. In all trials the maximum permitted tension is \(3mg\).

  1. Find the stretched length of the string, the radius of the circle and the speed of the particle.

    [4]

  2. For the same particle and string, find the range of possible values of \(\omega^2\) for steady non-degenerate circles respecting the tension limit.

    [4]

  3. The particle is replaced by one of mass \(2m\), but the same string is used. A steady circle at the angular speed from part (a) is proposed. Calculate its theoretical tension and angle to the vertical, and decide whether it is permitted.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

Length \(3a/2\), radius \(3\sqrt3a/4\), speed \(3\sqrt{ag}/2\).

(b)

\(\displaystyle \frac{4g}{5a}\lt\omega^2\leq\frac{12g}{7a}\).

(c)

Theoretical tension \(8mg\), angle \(\cos^{-1}(1/4)\); not permitted.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let the tension be \(T\), stretched length \(l\) and circle radius \(r\). Vertical balance gives \(T\cos60^\circ=mg\), so \(T=2mg\). Hooke's law gives \(2mg=4mg(l-a)/a\), hence \(l=3a/2\).

Thus \(r=l\sin60^\circ=3\sqrt3a/4\). Horizontally inwards, \[\frac{mv^2}{r}=T\sin60^\circ=\sqrt3mg.\] Consequently \(v^2=9ag/4\) and \(v=3\sqrt{ag}/2\).

Part (b)

In a general steady circle, \(T\sin\theta=m(l\sin\theta)\omega^2\). Since the circle is non-degenerate, \(\sin\theta\ne0\) and \(T=ml\omega^2\). Put \(\tau=T/(mg)\). Hooke's law gives \(l=a(1+\tau/4)\), hence \[\omega^2=\frac{4g}{a}\frac{\tau}{4+\tau}.\] Vertical balance gives \(\cos\theta=1/\tau\), so a non-degenerate circle requires \(\tau\gt1\). The force limit gives \(\tau\leq3\). The fraction \(\tau/(4+\tau)=1-4/(4+\tau)\) increases with \(\tau\), yielding the stated range. The lower endpoint corresponds to a zero-radius limiting position and is excluded.

Part (c)

From part (a), \(\omega^2=v^2/r^2=4g/(3a)\). The modulus remains \(4mg\), because the physical string has not changed. For the new mass, \[T=2ml\frac{4g}{3a}=\frac{8mg}{3a}l,\qquad T=\frac{4mg}{a}(l-a).\] Equating gives \(l=3a\), so \(T=8mg\). Vertical balance would then require \(8mg\cos\theta=2mg\), so \(\cos\theta=1/4\). Although the formal circle is geometrically possible, the force is above \(3mg\); the proposed trial is not permitted.
questions.hint_html: In a conical pendulum the circle radius is the horizontal projection of the stretched string length. Do not change the modulus when the mass changes.

questions.title: Removing a load: reconstructing the released position
questions.prompt_html:
A light spring of natural length \(1\,\mathrm m\) and modulus \(75\,\mathrm N\) is suspended vertically from a fixed point \(O\). A particle of mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), together with an additional load of mass \(M\,\mathrm{kg}\), hangs at rest from its lower end. The additional load is removed without giving the remaining particle an impulse. During its first upward motion, the particle has speed \(0.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at a distance \(1.52\,\mathrm m\) below \(O\). Use \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

  1. Find the new equilibrium length. Let \(q\) be downward displacement from that equilibrium and \(D\) its value immediately after removal. Show by energy that \(\frac32v^2+\frac{75}{2}q^2=\frac{75}{2}D^2\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(D\) and the removed mass \(M\).

    [4]

  3. Find the least distance below \(O\) reached by the particle, and the least tension during the motion.

    [3]

  4. Would replacing the spring by an elastic string with the same natural length and modulus alter this motion? Give a reasoned answer.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

New equilibrium length \(1.4\,\mathrm m\); the stated energy relation follows.

(b)

\(D=0.2\,\mathrm m\), \(M=1.5\,\mathrm{kg}\).

(c)

Least distance \(1.2\,\mathrm m\); least tension \(15\,\mathrm N\).

(d)

No, in the stated ideal model: the length remains between \(1.2\) and \(1.6\,\mathrm m\), so the string would always be stretched.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The stiffness is \(75\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\). After removal, equilibrium requires \(75e_0=30\), so \(e_0=0.4\,\mathrm m\) and the equilibrium length is \(1.4\,\mathrm m\).

At downward displacement \(q\), the change of total potential energy from its equilibrium value is \[\frac{75}{2}\big((0.4+q)^2-0.4^2\big)-30q=\frac{75}{2}q^2.\] The linear terms cancel because the reference position is equilibrium. Initially \(q=D\) and the speed is zero, so conservation of energy gives the required equation.

Part (b)

At the specified point, \(q=1.52-1.4=0.12\). Substitution gives \[D^2=0.12^2+\frac{3}{75}(0.8)^2=0.0144+0.0256=0.04.\] The old equilibrium was lower, so \(D=0.2\,\mathrm m\). The extra extension \(D\) supported the extra weight: \(75D=10M\). Therefore \(M=1.5\,\mathrm{kg}\).

Part (c)

At either turning point, \(v=0\), so \(q=\pm D\). The upper point has \(q=-0.2\), giving length \(1.4-0.2=1.2\,\mathrm m\). Its extension is \(0.2\,\mathrm m\), so the tension there is \(75(0.2)=15\,\mathrm N\). This is the least tension because the extension is least there.

Part (d)

The lower turning length is the initial length \(1.4+0.2=1.6\,\mathrm m\), and the upper turning length is \(1.2\,\mathrm m\). Throughout the motion the length exceeds \(1\,\mathrm m\). Therefore a replacement string never becomes slack and exerts exactly the same force as the spring at every position. The force law, initial position and initial speed are identical, so the predicted motion is identical. The conclusion would not be valid for a motion involving spring compression.

questions.title: A change of mass: compression or a slack phase?
questions.prompt_html:
A light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(kmg\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) on a smooth plane inclined at angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal, where \(\sin\alpha=3/5\). A particle of mass \(5m\) hangs down the line of greatest slope from \(O\), in equilibrium with spring length \(3a/2\). It is replaced by a particle of mass \(m\), held at the same position and then released from rest. The spring is constrained to remain straight and obeys Hooke's law in extension and compression.

  1. Find \(k\) and the new equilibrium length.

    [3]

  2. Use energy to find the greatest speed of the new particle and its distance from \(O\) when it next comes to rest.

    [5]

  3. Find the greatest magnitude of the spring force and the greatest magnitude of the acceleration during the motion.

    [3]

  4. In a separate trial replace the spring by an elastic string with the same natural length and modulus, keeping the release position unchanged. Find the distance from \(O\) at the next stop.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(k=6\); new equilibrium length \(11a/10\).

(b)

Greatest speed \(\frac{2\sqrt6}{5}\sqrt{ag}\); next resting position \(OP=7a/10\).

(c)

Greatest spring-force magnitude \(3mg\); greatest acceleration magnitude \(12g/5\).

(d)

\(OP=a/4\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Initially the tension is \(5mg(3/5)=3mg\). Since the extension is \(a/2\), Hooke's law gives \(kmg/2=3mg\), so \(k=6\). For the new particle, equilibrium requires \[\frac{6mg}{a}e_0=\frac35mg,\] so \(e_0=a/10\) and the new equilibrium length is \(11a/10\).

Part (b)

Let \(s=OP\) and let \(x=s-11a/10\). The total potential energy differs from its equilibrium value by \(3mgx^2/a\): the linear elastic term cancels the gravitational term. At release \(x=2a/5\). Thus \[\frac12mv^2+\frac{3mg}{a}x^2=\frac{3mg}{a}\left(\frac{2a}{5}\right)^2.\] The greatest speed occurs at \(x=0\), giving \(v^2=24ag/25\). At the next stop \(x=-2a/5\), so \(s=11a/10-2a/5=7a/10\). The spring is compressed by \(3a/10\) there, which is permitted for the stated spring model.

Part (c)

The signed extension ranges from \(-3a/10\) to \(a/2\). Therefore the largest absolute extension is \(a/2\), giving a spring-force magnitude \(3mg\).

The resultant along the plane is \(-6mgx/a\), so acceleration has magnitude \(6g|x|/a\). Its largest value is \(6g(2a/5)/a=12g/5\). The spring force alone is not the resultant; the component of weight must be included.

Part (d)

Until the length reaches \(a\), the force is unchanged. At \(s=a\), \(x=-a/10\), and the energy equation gives \(v^2=9ag/10\). The string is then slack. The particle continues up the plane with constant deceleration \(3g/5\), and travels a further distance \[d=\frac{9ag/10}{2(3g/5)}=\frac{3a}{4}.\] Thus the next stop is at \(OP=a-d=a/4\), before the particle reaches the attachment point. Compression energy must not be assigned to the slack string.

questions.title: A stretched string under a horizontal load
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of weight \(12\,\mathrm N\) is attached to a fixed point on a horizontal ceiling by a light elastic string of natural length \(1.2\,\mathrm m\) and modulus \(52\,\mathrm N\). A horizontal force of \(5\,\mathrm N\) maintains equilibrium. The string is straight and the particle is below the ceiling.

  1. Find the tension.

    [2]

  2. Find the vertical distance between the particle and the ceiling.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(13\,\mathrm N\).

(b)

\(18/13\,\mathrm m\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The vertical component of tension balances \(12\,\mathrm N\) and its horizontal component balances \(5\,\mathrm N\). These are perpendicular, so \[T=\sqrt{12^2+5^2}=13\,\mathrm N.\]

Part (b)

Hooke's law gives the extension \[e=\frac{Tl}{\lambda}=\frac{13(1.2)}{52}=0.3\,\mathrm m.\] The stretched length is \(1.5\,\mathrm m\). The vertical component of its unit direction is \(12/13\), so the vertical separation is \(1.5(12/13)=18/13\,\mathrm m\). The stretched length, not just the extension, must be projected vertically.

questions.title: Adding a stationary load to a hanging string
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(3M\) hangs in equilibrium from a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(8Mg\). A second particle of mass \(M\) is attached while the original particle is held fixed; the combined particle is then released from rest. No impulse or energy from an impact is involved.

  1. Find the speed after the combined particle has descended a distance \(a/8\).

    [4]

  2. Find the greatest extension reached.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\sqrt{ag/32}\).

(b)

\(5a/8\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The original equilibrium extension satisfies \(8Mg e_0/a=3Mg\), so \(e_0=3a/8\). After the specified descent it is \(a/2\). The new mass is \(4M\). The gravitational-energy loss is \(4Mg(a/8)=Mga/2\), while the elastic-energy increase is \[\frac{4Mg}{a}\left(\frac{a^2}{4}-\frac{9a^2}{64}\right)=\frac7{16}Mga.\] Hence \(\frac12(4M)v^2=Mga/16\), so \(v^2=ag/32\).

Part (b)

The new equilibrium extension is \(4Mg\cdot a/(8Mg)=a/2\). The total potential energy is a quadratic centred at \(a/2\). Its two equal-energy turning extensions therefore have sum \(a\). One is \(3a/8\), the release extension, so the other is \(5a/8\).

Equivalently, putting the downward displacement equal to \(d\) in the zero-speed energy equation gives \(4Mgd=(4Mg/a)[(3a/8+d)^2-(3a/8)^2]\), whose non-zero root is \(d=a/4\).
questions.hint_html: The additional mass changes the weight, but the extension cannot jump when it is attached.

questions.title: An unknown equilibrium length inferred after loading
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(2m\) hangs at rest from a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(kmg\). Its distance below the fixed end is \(x\), where \(x\gt a\). An additional particle of mass \(3m\) is attached without an impact while the original position is held, and the combined mass is then released from rest. After descending \(a/2\), its speed is \(\sqrt{ag/5}\).

  1. Express \(k\) in terms of \(x\) and \(a\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(x\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\displaystyle k=\frac{2a}{x-a}\).

(b)

\(x=5a/4\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At the original equilibrium the extension is \(x-a\), and Hooke's law gives a tension \(kmg(x-a)/a\). Balance this with the original weight \(2mg\): \[\frac{kmg}{a}(x-a)=2mg.\] Cancelling \(mg\) and rearranging gives \(k=2a/(x-a)\).

Part (b)

Put \(e_0=x-a=2a/k\). The gravitational-energy loss after the load is added is \(5mg(a/2)=5mga/2\). The kinetic energy at the measured position is \(\frac12(5m)(ag/5)=mga/2\). The elastic-energy increase is \[\frac{kmg}{2a}\left((e_0+a/2)^2-e_0^2\right)=mga+\frac{k}{8}mga,\] using \(ke_0/a=2\). Therefore \[\frac52=\frac12+1+\frac{k}{8},\] so \(k=8\), giving \(e_0=a/4\) and \(x=5a/4\).

The next stopping descent would be \(3a/4\), so the measured descent \(a/2\) is reached with positive speed before that stop.
questions.hint_html: Expanding the elastic-energy difference lets the initial equilibrium relation eliminate the unknown initial extension.

questions.title: Friction strong enough to prevent slackening
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) rests on a rough horizontal table and is joined to a fixed point \(A\) by a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(3mg\). It is held at \(AP=3a/2\), then released from rest. The coefficient of friction is \(\mu\), used both for sliding friction and for the limiting value of static friction.

  1. Find the range of \(\mu\) for which the particle starts moving but the string never becomes slack.

    [3]

  2. For \(\mu=1\), find the extension at the first stop and determine whether the particle remains there.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\displaystyle \frac34\leq\mu\lt\frac32\).

(b)

Extension \(a/6\); it remains at rest.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Initially the tension is \(3mg/2\), so motion starts only if \(\mu\lt3/2\). Initially the elastic energy is \(3mga/8\). To reach natural length the particle must travel \(a/2\) against friction, requiring work \(\mu mga/2\). It reaches natural length with no positive speed precisely when \(\mu\geq3/4\).

For \(3/4\leq\mu\lt3/2\), the first stopping extension obtained from energy is \(e_1=2\mu a/3-a/2\). Its tension is \((2\mu-3/2)mg\leq\mu mg\), so static friction can hold it. At \(\mu=3/4\), it stops exactly at natural length without passing into a slack interval.

Part (b)

If the final extension is \(e\), the distance travelled is \(a/2-e\). Work and energy give \[\frac38mga=\frac{3mg}{2a}e^2+mg\left(\frac a2-e\right).\] The roots are \(e=a/2\), the initial position, and \(e=a/6\), the first later stop. The tension there is \(mg/2\), below the available static-friction limit \(mg\). Static friction adjusts to \(mg/2\) away from \(A\), and the particle stays at rest.
questions.hint_html: A zero speed is not by itself proof of permanent rest. Compare the remaining tension with the maximum available static friction.

questions.title: Sliding friction is not the final static friction
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(mg\). The other end is fixed at \(O\) on a rough plane inclined at \(30^\circ\). The particle is released from rest at \(O\) and moves down a line of greatest slope. The magnitude of sliding friction is \(31mg/80\); the maximum available static friction is the same. The string does not obstruct the motion while slack.

  1. Find the distance travelled before the particle first comes to rest.

    [5]

  2. Determine the magnitude and direction of friction needed to keep the particle at rest there, and decide whether rest is possible.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(8a/5\).

(b)

\(mg/10\) down the plane; rest is possible.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The net work per unit distance from gravity and sliding friction is \[mg\sin30^\circ-\frac{31}{80}mg=\frac9{80}mg.\] This is positive, so the particle moves through the initial slack interval. If the later extension is \(e\), the total distance travelled is \(a+e\), not \(e\). At the first stop, \[\frac{mg}{2a}e^2=\frac9{80}mg(a+e).\] Writing \(z=e/a\) gives \(40z^2-9z-9=0=(5z-3)(8z+3)\). The physical root is \(z=3/5\), so the total distance is \(8a/5\).

During the taut phase the kinetic energy is \(mga[9(1+z)/80-z^2/2]\), positive for \(0\leq z\lt3/5\); the root found is the first stop.

Part (b)

At the stop the tension is \(mg(3a/5)/a=3mg/5\) uphill. The downhill weight component is \(mg/2\). Therefore a downhill frictional force of \[\frac35mg-\frac12mg=\frac1{10}mg\] is needed for equilibrium. This is less than \(31mg/80\), so it is available and the particle can remain at rest. Static friction is not automatically equal to its limiting value, and its direction here is opposite to its direction during the descent.
questions.hint_html: Work is done against friction even before the string becomes taut. At the final position, find the required static friction afresh.

questions.title: A rough-table launch from natural length
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(3mg\), fixed at a point on a rough horizontal table. The coefficient of friction is \(1/4\), both for sliding and for the limiting static value. With the string initially at natural length, the particle is projected directly away from the fixed end at speed \(\sqrt{ag}\).

  1. Find the greatest extension of the string.

    [4]

  2. Does the particle remain at this first stopping point?

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a/2\).

(b)

No. It begins moving back towards the fixed end.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let the extension at the first stop be \(e\). The particle has travelled distance \(e\), and friction has done negative work \(-mge/4\). Therefore \[\frac12mga=\frac{3mg}{2a}e^2+\frac14mge.\] With \(z=e/a\), this becomes \(6z^2+z-2=0=(3z+2)(2z-1)\). Extension must be non-negative, so \(z=1/2\) and \(e=a/2\).

Part (b)

The tension there is \(3mg/2\), larger than the maximum static friction \(mg/4\). The particle therefore cannot remain in equilibrium and starts moving towards the fixed end.
questions.hint_html: At the outward turning point, use work–energy first; then test whether static friction can hold the particle.

questions.title: Release from a compressed vertical spring
questions.prompt_html:
A light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(12mg\) has its lower end fixed on a horizontal plane. A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to its upper end. A smooth vertical guide keeps the spring straight without resisting vertical motion. The spring is compressed to length \(a/2\) and released from rest.

  1. Find the greatest extension above natural length.

    [4]

  2. Find the acceleration immediately after release.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a/3\).

(b)

\(5g\) upwards.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(x\) be signed extension, positive upwards from natural length. Total potential energy, apart from a constant, is \[U(x)=\frac{6mg}{a}x^2+mgx.\] Initially \(x=-a/2\), so \(U=mga\). At the upper turning point set \(x=za\) and \(K=0\): \[6z^2+z=1,\qquad (3z-1)(2z+1)=0.\] The root \(z=-1/2\) is the release point. The other root is \(z=1/3\), hence the greatest extension is \(a/3\).

Part (b)

The compressed spring pushes upwards with force \(12mg(a/2)/a=6mg\). After subtracting the weight, the resultant is \(5mg\) upwards, so the acceleration is \(5g\).
questions.hint_html: Compression stores positive elastic energy. Its force is upwards here, while extension would make the spring pull down.

questions.title: An upper turning point below natural length
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) hangs from a light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(8mg\), fixed at its upper end \(O\). The spring is constrained to remain straight. The particle is pulled down to a distance \(11a/8\) below \(O\) and released from rest.

  1. Find its distance below \(O\) when it next comes to rest, and state whether the spring is then stretched or compressed.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(7a/8\); compressed by \(a/8\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Use signed downward extension \(x\). The total potential energy is \(4mgx^2/a-mgx\), up to an additive constant. Initially \(x=3a/8\), giving \(U=3mga/16\). At a turning point, with \(z=x/a\), \[4z^2-z=\frac{3}{16},\qquad 64z^2-16z-3=0.\] The roots are \(3/8\) and \(-1/8\). The second is the next stop, so the full length is \(a-a/8=7a/8\). A spring can compress; replacing it by a string would require a different calculation once natural length is reached.
questions.hint_html: Use a signed extension for a spring; do not discard a negative extension merely because it is negative.

questions.title: Two speed measurements, one of them during compression
questions.prompt_html:
A light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(kmg\) lies along a smooth straight guide on a plane inclined at angle \(\alpha\), where \(\sin\alpha=4/5\). Its upper end is fixed at \(O\), and a particle of mass \(m\) is attached to its lower end. It is released from rest at \(OP=7a/4\). During the first ascent, its speed is \(V\) at \(OP=5a/4\), and \(V/2\) at \(OP=a/2\). The spring remains straight and can compress.

  1. Find \(k\).

    [5]

  2. Check that the particle can reach the second measured point before it next comes to rest.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(k=48/5\).

(b)

The next turning length is \(5a/12\), below \(a/2\), so the second point is reached.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At the first measured point the extension has changed from \(3a/4\) to \(a/4\), and the distance up the plane is \(a/2\). Therefore \[\frac{V^2}{2ag}=\frac{k}{2}\left(\frac9{16}-\frac1{16}\right)-\frac45\frac12=\frac{k}{4}-\frac25.\] At the second measured point the spring is compressed by \(a/2\), and the rise along the plane is \(5a/4\). Thus \[\frac{V^2}{8ag}=\frac{k}{2}\left(\frac9{16}-\frac14\right)-\frac45\frac54=\frac{5k}{32}-1.\] One quarter of the first right-hand side equals the second. Hence \(k/16-1/10=5k/32-1\), giving \(3k/32=9/10\), so \(k=48/5\).

Part (b)

The equilibrium signed extension is \(e_0=a\sin\alpha/k=a/12\). Total potential energy is a quadratic centred at \(e_0\), so the two zero-speed extensions satisfy \(e_1+e_2=2e_0\). With \(e_1=3a/4\), the other is \(e_2=a/6-3a/4=-7a/12\), giving length \(5a/12\).

The point \(OP=a/2\) occurs before that stop on the upward path. Also the first equation gives \(V^2=4ag\), so the speed at the second point is \(\sqrt{ag}\gt0\).
questions.hint_html: The energy of a compressed spring is positive. Keep track of the rise along the plane separately from the signed extension.

questions.title: Recovering the modulus from two speeds
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\), attached to a light elastic string of natural length \(a\), moves away from the fixed end on a smooth horizontal surface. Its speed is \(\sqrt{5ag}\) when the string length is \(5a/4\), and \(\sqrt{2ag}\) when the length is \(7a/4\). The modulus of elasticity is \(\lambda\).

  1. Find \(\lambda\).

    [3]

  2. Find the tension at the second measured point.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\lambda=6mg\).

(b)

\(9mg/2\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The extensions are \(a/4\) and \(3a/4\). The decrease in kinetic energy equals the increase in elastic energy: \[\frac12m(5ag-2ag)=\frac{\lambda}{2a}\left(\frac{9a^2}{16}-\frac{a^2}{16}\right)=\frac{\lambda a}{4}.\] Thus \(3mga/2=\lambda a/4\), giving \(\lambda=6mg\).

Part (b)

At extension \(3a/4\), \(T=6mg(3a/4)/a=9mg/2\).
questions.hint_html: Use the energy difference between the two observed positions; the initial launch speed is unnecessary.

questions.title: Energy and acceleration at a later extension
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(5mg\), fixed at a point \(O\) on a smooth horizontal table. It moves directly away from \(O\). Its speed is \(v\) at string length \(6a/5\), and \(2v/3\) at string length \(8a/5\).

  1. Find \(v\) in terms of \(a\) and \(g\).

    [4]

  2. Find the acceleration at the second measured point.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v=\frac{6\sqrt2}{5}\sqrt{ag}\).

(b)

\(3g\) towards \(O\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The extensions are \(a/5\) and \(3a/5\). Energy conservation gives \[\frac12m\left(v^2-\frac49v^2\right)=\frac{5mg}{2a}\left(\frac{9a^2}{25}-\frac{a^2}{25}\right).\] Thus \(5mv^2/18=4mga/5\), so \(v^2=72ag/25\). Taking the positive square root gives the stated speed. The factor \(2/3\) in speed must be squared in the kinetic energy.

Part (b)

At extension \(3a/5\), the tension is \(5mg(3a/5)/a=3mg\). This is the only horizontal force, directed towards \(O\), so the acceleration is \(3g\) towards \(O\).
questions.hint_html: Energy relates the two speeds, whereas the instantaneous acceleration comes from the force at the later position.

questions.title: A numerical inclined-plane energy problem
questions.prompt_html:
A light elastic string of natural length \(0.6\,\mathrm m\) and modulus \(30\,\mathrm N\) lies along a line of greatest slope on a smooth plane. Its upper end is fixed. A particle of mass \(1.5\,\mathrm{kg}\) is attached to its lower end. The plane makes angle \(\alpha\) with the horizontal, where \(\sin\alpha=4/5\). Starting with the string at natural length, the particle is projected down the plane at speed \(\sqrt{12/5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Use \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

  1. Find the greatest extension.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(0.6\,\mathrm m\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let the greatest extension be \(e\) metres. Initial kinetic energy is \(\frac12(1.5)(12/5)=9/5\,\mathrm J\). The downhill weight component is \(1.5(10)(4/5)=12\,\mathrm N\), so the gravitational-energy loss is \(12e\,\mathrm J\). At the first stop, \[\frac95+12e=\frac{30e^2}{2(0.6)}=25e^2.\] Thus \(125e^2-60e-9=0=(5e-3)(25e+3)\). Only \(e=3/5\) is non-negative. The greatest extension is \(0.6\,\mathrm m\); the full stretched length is \(1.2\,\mathrm m\).
questions.hint_html: Keep SI units throughout. Gravitational energy is released as the particle travels down the plane.

questions.title: Recovering an unknown release extension
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(8mg\), suspended vertically from a fixed point. It is pulled down and released from rest at extension \(e\), where \(e\gt a/4\). After rising \(a/4\), its speed is \(\sqrt{3ag/2}\).

  1. Find \(e\).

    [4]

  2. Find the greatest speed in this first upward motion.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(e=5a/8\).

(b)

\(\sqrt{2ag}\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Since \(e\gt a/4\), the string is still stretched at the measured point. The elastic-energy decrease supplies the kinetic energy and the gravitational-energy increase: \[\frac{4mg}{a}\left(e^2-(e-a/4)^2\right)=\frac12m\frac{3ag}{2}+mg\frac a4.\] The right-hand side is \(mga\). The left-hand side simplifies to \(2mge-mga/4\). Hence \(2e-a/4=a\), giving \(e=5a/8\), which satisfies the stated inequality.

Part (b)

The resultant is zero when the tension equals the weight, at extension \(a/8\). Relative to that position, the release displacement is \(5a/8-a/8=a/2\). The available energy is \(\frac12(8mg/a)(a/2)^2=mga\). Thus \(\frac12mv_{\max}^2=mga\), so \(v_{\max}=\sqrt{2ag}\). The speed decreases after this position, including any later slack phase of the ascent.
questions.hint_html: At the observation point the extension is e minus the distance risen, not the full string length minus that distance.

questions.title: Returning to natural length is not the end of the motion
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(4mg\), fixed vertically at its upper end \(O\). A smooth vertical guide keeps the spring straight and allows compression. The particle is released from rest when the spring extension is \(3a/4\).

  1. Find the initial acceleration.

    [2]

  2. Find the speed when the spring first returns to natural length.

    [3]

  3. Find the least length of the spring during the motion.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(2g\) upwards.

(b)

\(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sqrt{ag}\).

(c)

\(3a/4\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The initial tension is \(4mg(3a/4)/a=3mg\). The upward resultant is therefore \(3mg-mg=2mg\), giving acceleration \(2g\) upwards.

Part (b)

The initial elastic energy is \(\frac{4mg}{2a}(3a/4)^2=9mga/8\). The rise to natural length costs \(3mga/4\), so \[\frac12mv^2=\frac98mga-\frac34mga=\frac38mga.\] Hence \(v^2=3ag/4\), giving the stated speed. Natural length is passed with non-zero speed.

Part (c)

For signed downward extension \(x\), the turning-point equation is \(2mgx^2/a-mgx=3mga/8\). Its roots are \(x=3a/4\) and \(x=-a/4\). The latter gives the upper turning point, with spring length \(3a/4\). The negative extension is compression, not a slack interval.
questions.hint_html: The spring still acts after it becomes shorter than natural length; a string would not.

questions.title: Finding an incline from the turning length
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) lies on a smooth plane inclined at an acute angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal. It is attached to the upper end of the plane by a light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(4mg\), along a line of greatest slope. It is released from rest with the spring at natural length. The greatest spring length is \(4a/3\).

  1. Find \(\theta\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\theta=\sin^{-1}(2/3)\), approximately \(41.8^\circ\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The particle descends \(a/3\) along the plane, and stops at extension \(a/3\). Gravitational energy lost equals elastic energy gained: \[mg\frac a3\sin\theta=\frac{4mg}{2a}\left(\frac a3\right)^2.\] Thus \(\sin\theta=2/3\). Since the angle is acute, \(\theta=\sin^{-1}(2/3)\approx41.8^\circ\).
questions.hint_html: The maximum length is not the maximum extension.

questions.title: The first of two equal-speed passages
questions.prompt_html:
A light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(6mg\) is fixed at its upper end. Particles of masses \(m\) and \(5m\) hang together in equilibrium at its lower end. The \(5m\) particle is removed without imparting an impulse. The remaining particle moves vertically upwards.

  1. Find the string length when the speed of the remaining particle first reaches \(2\sqrt{ag}\).

    [4]

  2. Find the greatest speed in this first upward motion.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(4a/3\).

(b)

\(\frac5{\sqrt6}\sqrt{ag}\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Initially the total weight is \(6mg\), so the extension is \(a\). After the mass is removed, the release length is therefore \(2a\), and the initial elastic energy is \(3mga\).

Put the later extension equal to \(za\), while the string is taut. The particle has risen by \((1-z)a\), so \[\frac12mv^2=3mga-mga(1-z)-3mga z^2=mga(2+z-3z^2).\] For \(v=2\sqrt{ag}\), this gives \(z-3z^2=0\). The roots are \(z=1/3\) and \(z=0\). During the first ascent, \(z\) decreases from 1, so the first passage is at \(z=1/3\), with length \(4a/3\).

Part (b)

Complete the square in the energy expression: \[2+z-3z^2=\frac{25}{12}-3\left(z-\frac16\right)^2.\] The largest kinetic energy is \(25mga/12\), attained at \(z=1/6\), so \(v_{\max}^2=25ag/6\). This point is reached before the string becomes slack. In the subsequent slack phase the particle continues upwards against gravity and slows down.
questions.hint_html: After removal, the moving mass changes but the initial extension does not. A speed can occur twice on the ascent.

questions.title: Crossing the attachment point on a smooth incline
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) moves along a smooth straight guide on a plane inclined at angle \(\alpha\), where \(\sin\alpha=3/4\). It is attached to a fixed point \(O\) of the guide by a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(3mg\). Initially the particle is held uphill of \(O\), a distance \(5a/4\) from \(O\), and released from rest. The idealised attachment does not obstruct the particle as it passes \(O\); the string is slack whenever its end separation is less than \(a\).

  1. Find the position where the speed is greatest during the first descent.

    [3]

  2. Find that greatest speed.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(5a/4\) downhill of \(O\).

(b)

\(\frac{\sqrt{15}}2\sqrt{ag}\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Above \(O\), gravity and any string tension both act downhill. While the string is slack, the downhill acceleration is \(3g/4\). Below \(O\), after the separation exceeds \(a\), the tension acts uphill. The speed is greatest when the resultant first becomes zero: \[\frac{3mg}{a}(s-a)=\frac34mg.\] Thus \(s=5a/4\), measured downhill from \(O\). Before this point the acceleration is downhill; immediately after it the acceleration is uphill, so this is genuinely a maximum speed.

Part (b)

The string extension is \(a/4\) both at release and at the maximum-speed point. Hence the elastic energies cancel in the energy difference. The total distance down the plane is \(5a/2\), and the vertical drop is \((5a/2)(3/4)=15a/8\). Therefore \[\frac12mv^2=\frac{15}{8}mga,\] so \(v^2=15ag/4\). No elastic energy is assigned to the slack part of the journey; comparing the endpoints remains valid because there is no dissipation.

questions.title: Just reaching the suspension point
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) hangs in equilibrium from a light elastic string of natural length \(3a\) and modulus \(3mg\), fixed at a point \(O\). It is pulled vertically down a further distance \(d\) and released from rest. The value of \(d\) is such that the particle just reaches \(O\) with zero speed during its first ascent. Consider the motion only up to that event.

  1. Find \(d\) in terms of \(a\).

    [5]

  2. Find the speed when the particle first reaches the natural-length position.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(d=\sqrt7a\).

(b)

\(\sqrt{6ag}\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At equilibrium the extension is \(a\), so the equilibrium distance below \(O\) is \(4a\). The release length is \(4a+d\) and its extension is \(a+d\).

At \(O\), the string is slack and both its elastic energy and the particle's kinetic energy are zero. Taking gravitational potential zero at \(O\), conservation of energy gives \[\frac{3mg}{2(3a)}(a+d)^2-mg(4a+d)=0.\] Thus \((a+d)^2=2a(4a+d)\), which reduces to \(d^2=7a^2\). Since the particle is pulled down, \(d=\sqrt7a\).

The particle first rises while the string is taut and then continues in free vertical motion. An elastic-energy expression for a compressed spring would be invalid here.

Part (b)

At the natural-length position the particle is \(3a\) below \(O\). It must subsequently rise \(3a\) with no elastic force and finish with zero speed. Therefore \[\frac12mv^2=3mga,\] so \(v=\sqrt{6ag}\). This also confirms that natural length is passed with positive speed and that the final zero-speed event is at \(O\), not earlier.
questions.hint_html: At the suspension point an elastic string has no compression energy. Use the total rise from release, then examine the natural-length boundary.

questions.title: A speed measured after the string has become slack
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(4mg\), fixed at its upper end \(O\). It is held vertically below \(O\) with the string length \(5a/2\), then released from rest. Consider only its first upward motion below \(O\).

  1. Find its speed when it is \(a/2\) below \(O\).

    [3]

  2. Find the acceleration immediately after release.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\sqrt{5ag}\).

(b)

\(5g\) upwards.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The initial extension is \(3a/2\), so the stored elastic energy is \[\frac{4mg}{2a}\left(\frac{3a}{2}\right)^2=\frac92mga.\] At the requested point the string is slack and has zero elastic energy. The particle has risen by \(2a\). Therefore \[\frac12mv^2=\frac92mga-2mga=\frac52mga,\] so \(v=\sqrt{5ag}\). The positive value confirms that this point is reached before the particle stops.

Part (b)

Initially the tension is \(4mg(3a/2)/a=6mg\). Subtract the weight to obtain an upward resultant \(5mg\), hence an acceleration \(5g\).

questions.title: Launching upwards from the fixed end of a string
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and unknown modulus \(\lambda\). Its other end is fixed at \(O\). The particle is projected vertically upwards from \(O\); the string is initially slack. While rising at a height \(3a/2\) above \(O\), the particle has speed \(\sqrt{11ag/2}\) and acceleration \(4g\) downwards. The idealised fixed end does not obstruct the launch.

  1. Find \(\lambda\).

    [2]

  2. Find the launch speed.

    [2]

  3. Find the greatest height above \(O\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\lambda=6mg\).

(b)

\(\sqrt{10ag}\).

(c)

\(2a\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At height \(3a/2\), the extension is \(a/2\). Both tension and weight act downwards, so \(T+mg=4mg\), giving \(T=3mg\). Since \(T=\lambda(a/2)/a=\lambda/2\), the modulus is \(\lambda=6mg\).

Part (b)

At the measured position, kinetic energy is \(11mga/4\), gravitational energy above \(O\) is \(3mga/2\), and elastic energy is \(\frac{6mg}{2a}(a/2)^2=3mga/4\). Their sum is \(5mga\). At launch the string has zero elastic energy, so \(\frac12mu^2=5mga\), giving \(u=\sqrt{10ag}\).

Part (c)

The greatest height is beyond the measured point, so the string is taut there. Write the height as \(a(1+z)\), with \(z\gt1/2\). At the upper turning point kinetic energy is zero, so \[mga(1+z)+3mga z^2=5mga.\] Thus \(3z^2+z-4=0=(3z+4)(z-1)\). Only \(z=1\) is physically admissible, yielding height \(2a\). During the ascent the acceleration is always downward, both in the slack phase and after tension starts, so this is the unique upper turning point.
questions.hint_html: The string pulls down when the particle is above O. Its elastic energy is zero throughout the initial slack interval.

questions.title: A symmetric suspension that only just reaches the supports
questions.prompt_html:
Fixed points \(A\) and \(B\) are at the same level and \(6a\) apart. A uniform light elastic string of natural length \(6a\) and modulus \(\lambda\) has its ends attached to \(A\) and \(B\). A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to its midpoint. Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(AB\). In equilibrium the particle is \(4a\) vertically below \(M\). Each half of the string has natural length \(3a\) and the same modulus \(\lambda\).

  1. Find \(\lambda\).

    [3]

  2. The particle is pulled down to \(36a/5\) below \(M\) and released from rest. Show that it reaches \(M\) with zero speed. Explain why it does not stop earlier.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\lambda=15mg/16\).

(b)

It first stops at \(M\), with speed zero.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At equilibrium each half has length \(\sqrt{(3a)^2+(4a)^2}=5a\), hence extension \(2a\). Each tension is \(T=2\lambda/3\). The vertical component of each tension is \(4T/5\), so \[2\left(\frac{4T}{5}\right)=mg.\] Thus \(T=5mg/8\), and \(\lambda=(3/2)T=15mg/16\). The modulus is not halved when a uniform string is divided into halves.

Part (b)

At release each half has length \[\sqrt{9a^2+\frac{1296}{25}a^2}=\frac{39a}{5},\] so each extension is \(24a/5\). The total elastic energy is \[2\frac{\lambda(24a/5)^2}{2(3a)}=\frac{36}{5}mga.\] At \(M\) the string is at natural length and this energy is exactly the gravitational gain \(36mga/5\). Hence the speed at \(M\) is zero.

For a downward separation \(h\), the upward elastic resultant is \[\frac{2\lambda}{3a}\left(h-\frac{3ah}{\sqrt{9a^2+h^2}}\right).\] It increases strictly with \(h\gt0\) and equals \(mg\) only at \(h=4a\). Thus the total potential energy has its unique minimum there: it decreases from the release position to equilibrium and then increases to its value at \(M\). It is strictly below the release energy at every intermediate point, so there is no earlier stop. At \(M\), gravity acts downwards and the particle reverses direction.
questions.hint_html: Use the energy of both half-strings. Equal initial and final total energies are not sufficient unless the intermediate path is accessible.
