questions.title: A guided circular path with a spring and a holding force
questions.prompt_html:
Points \(A\) and \(B\) are fixed at the same horizontal level, with \(AB=5a\). A particle \(P\) of mass \(m\) is attached to \(A\) by a light rigid rod of length \(4a\), smoothly pivoted at \(A\). It is also joined to \(B\) by a light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(kmg\). Everything lies in one vertical plane.

Initially, taking \(A=(0,0)\), \(B=(5a,0)\) and upward positive, the particle is held at \(P=(16a/5,-12a/5)\) by a vertical force \(F\). When \(F\) is removed, the particle moves from rest towards the position \(P=(4a,0)\). Its speed there is \(\sqrt{16ag/5}\).

  1. Find \(k\).

    [4]

  2. Find the magnitude and direction of the force \(F\) before release.

    [3]

  3. Find the force in the rod immediately before release, and state whether it is tensile or compressive.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(k=2\).

(b)

\(4mg\) vertically downwards.

(c)

\(3mg\), tensile.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Initially \(BP=\sqrt{(9a/5)^2+(12a/5)^2}=3a\), so the spring extension is \(2a\). At \(P=(4a,0)\), the spring has natural length \(a\). The particle has risen by \(12a/5\). The rod force does no work because it is perpendicular to the allowed displacement. Therefore \[\frac{kmg}{2a}(2a)^2=mg\frac{12a}{5}+\frac12m\frac{16ag}{5}.\] Thus \(2k=12/5+8/5=4\), so \(k=2\). The stated rise costs gravitational energy; it is not a fall.

Part (b)

Initially the spring tension is \((2mg/a)(2a)=4mg\). The lengths \(AP=4a\), \(BP=3a\), \(AB=5a\) form a right-angled triangle, so the spring is perpendicular to the rod. Resolve perpendicular to the rod, in the direction of the spring force. The component of an upward vertical force in this direction is \(4/5\) of its magnitude.

Taking \(F\) as signed upwards, equilibrium perpendicular to the rod gives \[4mg-\frac45mg+\frac45F=0.\] Therefore \(F=-4mg\): the holding force has magnitude \(4mg\) and acts downwards. The rod force has no component in this resolution direction.

Part (c)

Horizontal equilibrium gives \(4mg(3/5)-R(4/5)=0\), hence \(R=3mg\). The assumed force was towards \(A\), and the result is positive, so the rod is in tension. This is a static force immediately before removal of \(F\); a radial-acceleration term must not be inserted at that instant.
questions.hint_html: Use the explicitly given coordinates for the two direction triangles. The holding force can act downwards; do not assume its direction.

questions.title: A coalescing impact followed by spring compression
questions.prompt_html:
A particle \(P\) of mass \(m\) is attached to a light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(6mg\), whose other end is fixed at \(O\) on a smooth horizontal table. Initially \(P\) is at rest and the spring is at natural length. A second particle \(Q\), of mass \(km\), approaches \(P\) along the spring line towards \(O\), at speed \(2\sqrt{ag}\). They collide and stick together. The greatest compression reached subsequently is \(a/3\). The spring is kept straight.

  1. Find \(k\).

    [4]

  2. Find the kinetic energy lost in the collision.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(k=1/2\).

(b)

\(2mga/3\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

During the short collision the elastic force has no appreciable impulse. If the common speed immediately afterwards is \(U\), conservation of momentum gives \[km(2\sqrt{ag})=(1+k)mU,\qquad U=\frac{2k}{1+k}\sqrt{ag}.\] Kinetic energy is not conserved in this sticking collision. It is conserved with elastic potential energy in the subsequent smooth motion: \[\frac12(1+k)mU^2=\frac{6mg}{2a}\left(\frac a3\right)^2=\frac13mga.\] Substitution gives \(6k^2=1+k\), or \((3k+1)(2k-1)=0\). Since the mass is positive, \(k=1/2\).

Part (b)

Initially the kinetic energy is \(\frac12(\frac12m)(2\sqrt{ag})^2=mga\). Immediately after the collision it is \(mga/3\), equal to the later maximum elastic energy. Therefore the collision loss is \(mga-mga/3=2mga/3\).
questions.hint_html: Use momentum for the impact, then energy for the subsequent compression. Do not conserve mechanical energy across a sticking collision.

questions.title: An impact, a smooth section and the edge of a rough strip
questions.prompt_html:
A light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(6mg\) has one end fixed at \(O\) on a horizontal table and the other attached to a particle \(A\) of mass \(km\). Initially it is at natural length and \(A\) is at rest. A particle \(B\) of mass \(m\) strikes \(A\) directly towards \(O\) with speed \(\sqrt{3ag/2}\); the particles stick together. The spring remains straight.

The motion is smooth until the combined particle reaches \(C\), where the spring length is \(3a/4\). Immediately before reaching \(C\) its speed is half the speed immediately after the collision. At \(C\) it enters a rough strip on the side nearer \(O\), with coefficient of sliding friction \(\mu\). There is no impact or step at the boundary. Immediately after entering the strip its deceleration is \(3g/4\).

  1. Find \(k\).

    [6]

  2. Find \(\mu\), explaining what happens to the speed and acceleration at the boundary of the strip.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(k=2\).

(b)

\(\mu=1/4\). Speed is continuous; the deceleration changes from \(g/2\) to \(3g/4\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(u=\sqrt{3ag/2}\), and let \(U\) be the common speed after collision. Momentum gives \(mu=(k+1)mU\), so \(U=u/(k+1)\).

Before the rough strip, the compression at \(C\) is \(a/4\). Energy lost from the combined particle's motion is stored in the spring: \[\frac12(k+1)m\left(U^2-\frac{U^2}{4}\right)=\frac{6mg}{2a}\left(\frac a4\right)^2=\frac3{16}mga.\] Substituting \(U^2=3ag/[2(k+1)^2]\) gives \(9/[16(k+1)]=3/16\). Hence \(k+1=3\), and \(k=2\). The common speed at \(C\) is \(u/6\).

Part (b)

At \(C\), the spring pushes away from \(O\) with force \(6mg(a/4)/a=3mg/2\). The combined mass is \(3m\), so immediately before the boundary the deceleration is \(g/2\).

After entry, friction \(3\mu mg\) also acts away from \(O\), opposing the motion. Hence \[\frac32mg+3\mu mg=3m\frac{3g}{4},\] which gives \(\mu=1/4\). There is no impulsive force at the boundary, so the speed cannot jump. The force, and therefore the acceleration, changes discontinuously as friction starts to act.
questions.hint_html: At C the spring is compressed, so its force and friction act in the same direction. Neither an energy loss nor a speed jump occurs at a zero-width boundary without an impulse.
